title.en: Guna: The Lion Who Repaid the Jackal

region.en: A mountain cave above the waters below the Himalaya (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 雪山下山水之間的山洞（象徵標記）

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: After a jackal digs him out of the mud, a lion takes the jackal's family into his own cave; when the lioness bullies them out of groundless jealousy, the lion rebukes her -- a friend who played a friendly part is flesh and blood, whatever his size -- and the friendship of the two families endures through seven generations.
summary.zh: 獅子撲鹿失足陷入泥沼七日，胡狼為之掘泥引水，救其脫困。獅子遂迎胡狼一家入洞同居，共獵同食，兩家幼崽一同長大。母獅疑忌，乘獅外出凌虐胡狼之妻。胡狼請辭，獅子斥妻：『救命之友，雖小亦親』，並誦偈明志。此後兩家親善，友誼延續七代。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: When Elder Ananda received a thousand robes from the ladies of the king's palace and gave them all away, the king at first took offence, till Ananda explained that no gift of the faithful is wasted -- the robe becomes a cloak, the cloak a shirt, the shirt a coverlet, the coverlet a mat, the mat a towel, and the towel's shreds are mixed with clay for mortar. Pleased, the king gave the other five hundred robes; and when the Brethren asked why the Elder had favoured his own young attendant with them, the Master told a story of gratitude in olden times.

A lion living in a cave on the hills leapt at a deer grazing on the soft grass by the water, and came down in the mud, where he stuck fast for seven days with his feet fixed like four posts. A jackal hunting for food saw him and ran in terror; but the lion called out, 'Don't run -- here am I, caught fast in the mud; please save me!' 'I could pull you out, but I much fear that once out you might eat me.' 'Fear nothing; I will do you great service.' So the jackal worked away the mud, dug channels for the water, struck the lion's belly from beneath with his head, and the lion scrambled out.

The lion killed a buffalo, fed the jackal, took a piece home for his own mate, and settled the jackal's family in a cave by the entrance of his own; the two hunted together, and the she-jackal and the lioness each bore two cubs. But the lioness grew jealous and, when the hunters were away, plagued and terrified the jackal's mate. 'We have outstayed our welcome,' said the she-jackal to her husband, 'let us go back to our old place.' The jackal told the lion: 'The strong will always have their way; I fear what once I trusted to.' Then the lion said to his mate, 'This jackal saved my life; a friend who plays a friendly part, however small and weak he be, is my kinsman and my flesh and blood. Never again put a slight upon my comrade, or his wife, or his family.' The two households made their peace, and the friendship remained unbroken through seven generations.

title.en: Mora: The Golden Peacock

region.en: The golden hill of Dandaka in the Himalaya marches, and Benares (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喜馬拉雅邊地檀陀迦金山與波羅奈城（象徵標記）

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: A golden peacock guards himself at dawn and dusk with hymns to the sun; six kings' hunters die trying to snare him for a queen's dream and for a gilded lie about immortal flesh. A seventh hunter trains a dancing peahen, and desire -- the charm unsaid -- loses the peacock his freedom, until in Benares he proves a former glory by a chariot dug out of the lake.
summary.zh: 金孔雀日誦晨昏二咒以自護，獵人布羅七年不得近，女王與獵人皆死。繼位諸王見金版刻文，謂食其肉者長生不老，迭遣獵人皆無功。第七王之獵人馴一母孔雀為餌，孔雀見雌起貪，晨咒未誦而落網。至波羅奈，孔雀自述前世為轉輪王持五戒故得金色，並令掘王湖得寶車為證，國王遂受教化。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: A golden peacock, hatched from a shell yellow as a kanikara bud, settled on a plateau of a golden hill in Dandaka after traversing three ranges of hills. At dawn, watching the sun rise, he composed a spell to preserve himself: 'There he rises, king all-seeing, making all things bright with his golden light; thee I worship, glorious being; keep me safe through the coming day' -- and at evening, when he sat upon the hilltop, a second spell beginning 'There he sets.' Between the spells he honoured the departed Buddhas and all their virtues, then went a-feeding.

A hunter of a wild village near Benares found him and told his son; and Queen Khema, dreaming that a golden peacock was holding a religious discourse, longed to hear it. The first hunter set snares for seven years; but even when the peacock stepped upon them they would not close, and the hunter died, and the queen died unfulfilled. The king caused a golden plate to be inscribed: whoso eats of the flesh of the golden peacock of Dandaka becomes ever young and immortal. King after king -- six in all -- sent hunters and read the plate; all failed and died.

The seventh king's hunter marked that the bird recited a charm before feeding, trapped a peahen, and trained her to dance at a clap and cry at a snap of the fingers. Setting the snare before dawn, he made the peahen utter her note; unwonted desire woke in the peacock's breast, he came with his charm unsaid, and was caught. Brought to Benares, he told the king that his flesh could not give immortality to the eater once he died, and that his golden colour came from keeping the Five Commandments as a universal monarch in a former life. For proof he bade the king drain the royal lake, where his jewelled chariot of that reign lay buried; dug up, it convinced the king, who took the peacock's teaching on impermanence, gave him his kingdom and the highest honours, and sent him back to Dandaka with the parting word 'Be careful!'

title.en: Indasamanagotta: The Pet Elephant
title.zh: 因陀沙摩那各多本生：寵象之禍

region.en: A company of anchorites in the Himalaya region (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喜馬拉雅地區苦行僧團（象徵標記）

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: Against his teacher's plain warning an anchorite rears a motherless elephant; when the south wind brings the frenzy of musth, the beast smashes the hermitage, waits watching in the thicket, and dashes its foster-father to death as he comes laden with its food.
summary.zh: 僧團中有一執拗不馴者名因陀沙摩那，養一失母幼象。師菩薩誡之：『象長成後，雖養育之恩亦不能免其害，宜早棄之。』彼不聽。一日僧眾遠行採果，南風起，象狂性大發，毀舍砸罐，入林伺候。主人攜食先歸，方欲近前，象衝出，捲之擲地，一擊斃命，狂鳴遁去。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: Among five hundred anchorites in the Himalayas led by the Bodhisatta was a headstrong and unteachable person named Indasamanagotta, who kept a pet elephant which had lost its dam. The teacher sent for him: 'When elephants grow up, they kill even those who foster them; you had better not keep it any longer.' 'But I cannot live without him, my Teacher!' 'Oh, well; you will live to repent it.' Still he reared the creature, and by and by it grew to an immense size.

It happened once that the anchorites all went far afield to gather roots and fruits, and were absent several days. At the first breath of the south wind the elephant fell into a frenzy: 'Destruction to this hut! I will smash the water-jar, overturn the stone bench, tear up the pallet, kill the hermit, and then be off!' So he sped into the jungle, and waited watching for their return.

The master came first, laden with food for his pet, and hastened up thinking all was well, as at their usual meeting. Out rushed the elephant from the thicket, seized him in his trunk, dashed him to the ground, and with one blow on the head crushed the life out of him; then, madly trumpeting, he scampered into the forest. The other anchorites brought the news to the Bodhisatta, who said, 'We should have no dealings with the bad,' and repeated his verses: friendship with evil let the good eschew; they work mischief, be it soon or late, even as the elephant his master slew. He performed the dead man's obsequies, and taught his band that it is well to be docile and not obstinate.

title.en: Satadhamma: The Leavings of a Low-Caste Man
title.zh: 薩吒達摩本生：賤民餘飯

region.en: The high road north out of Benares in the Kasi country
region.zh: 迦尸國波羅奈城北行大道

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: A high-born brahmin sneers at his low-caste travelling companion's rice, but hunger by nightfall drives him to beg the leavings; choking with shame he vomits blood, plunges into the jungle and dies -- while the Buddha warns Brethren who live by unlawful means that food so won leaves neither laughter nor joy.
summary.zh: 高貴婆羅門青年薩吒達摩與賤民旅伴同行。午間賤民以飯相讓，彼斥曰『不需，你這賤民』。晚間沐浴後飢不可忍，眼睜睜看對方進食，終開口討殘飯，剔除污穢而食之。食畢自思：辱及出身氏族！嘔血懊悔，遁入叢林，無人再見，死於其中。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: A young brahmin named Satadhamma, son of a magnifico of the north, took the road out of Benares, and fell in with a man of the lowest caste who carried some rice grains in a basket. 'Let us journey together,' said the brahmin. At breakfast time the low-born man sat by good water, washed his hands, opened his basket and offered a share. 'Tut, tut,' said the other, 'I want none, you low fellow.' The Bodhisatta wasted nothing, ate, drank, washed, and picked up the rest of his rice.

At evening, after a bath in nice water, the low-born man sat down and began to eat, this time offering nothing. The young gentleman, tired with walking all day and hungry to the bottom of his soul, stood looking on, thinking, 'If he offers me any, I will take it.' But the other ate without a word. 'Well, I will beg a piece; I can throw away the outside, which is defiled, and eat the rest.' So he did; and as soon as he had eaten he thought, 'How I have disgraced my birth, my clan, my family! I have eaten the leavings of a low-born churl.' Keen remorse seized him; he threw up the food, and blood came with it.

'What a trifle! and his leavings! given too against his will! And I a highborn brahmin! and the stuff has made me ill!' he lamented. 'Why did I do such a wicked thing just for life's sake?' He plunged into the jungle and was never seen again by any eye, but died there forlorn. The Master drew the moral for Brethren who earned their living in unlawful ways: food so won is like a piece of red-hot iron, like a deadly poison, and for those who partake of it there is no laughter and no joy.

title.en: Asadisa: Prince Peerless the Archer
title.zh: 無比王子本生：神箭退七王

region.en: Benares in the Kasi country, and a neighbouring royal court
region.zh: 迦尸國波羅奈城與鄰國王庭

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: Robbed of his throne by slaves' slander, Prince Peerless serves a foreign king at a peerless wage; one arrow flung to the heaven of the Four Great Kings, another to the Thirty-three, bring down a mango cluster to the wonder of all -- and later a single inscribed arrow into the seven besieging kings' golden dish puts them to flight without shedding a fly's drink of blood.
summary.zh: 無比王子遭宮奴讒害，流落他國，以十萬年薪受聘為弓手。園中取果一試神技：第一箭直上天宮釘穿果柄，第二箭追上其羽折返，落箭聲如雷霆，一髮不差剖斷果簇，觀者以為神人，獲賞千萬。後七王圍其故國，王弟急召兄長。王子刻字於箭：『無比王子歸矣，一箭必盡誅爾等』，射入七王共食之金盤，七王嚇遁，不流蠅飲之血。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: Prince Peerless, so named by soothsayers at his birth, was taught the Three Vedas and the Eighteen Accomplishments at Takkasila and became peerless in archery. His father dying, the kingship was offered to him, but he refused it, and his younger brother Brahmadatta was consecrated in his stead. Then slaves slandered Peerless to the new king -- 'Prince Peerless wants to be king!' -- and the king believed them and sent men to take him prisoner. Warned, the prince went away in anger to another country and entered the service of its king at a hundred thousand a year, to the grumbling of the old archers.

In the royal park the king coveted a mango cluster too high to climb, and the jealous archers deflected the task to the newcomer. Peerless asked to shoot from the couch's place, went behind a screen, and donned mail and turban, with his great ramshorn bow. 'Am I to bring this fruit down with an upward shot, or by dropping the arrow upon it?' 'Never saw I a mark taken in the fall; make the shaft fall on it.' 'This arrow will fly high, up to the heaven of the Four Great Kings, and return; a second will follow faster and turn it back. Be patient till it returns.' The first arrow pierced the stalk exactly in the middle; the second struck the first's feathers; the deities of the Thirty-three caught and kept the second shaft.

The falling arrow cleft the air with a thunderclap, and the crowd fell flat for fear; down it came, not a hair's-breadth out either way, cut the stalk of the cluster, and the archer caught arrow in one hand and fruit in the other. Thousands of kerchiefs waved, the courtiers showered ten millions of money, and the king honours fell like rain. Meanwhile seven kings, knowing there was no Prince Peerless in Benares, drew a leaguer round the city and summoned its king to fight or yield; the frightened king sent messengers to his brother. Peerless returned, comforted him, and scratched on an arrow: 'I, Prince Peerless, am returned; I mean to kill you all with one arrow which I will shoot at you; let those who care for life make their escape.' The arrow fell on the very middle of the golden dish at which the seven kings were eating together, and they fled half-dead. The prince then forsook the world and came at his life's end to Brahma's heaven.

title.en: Silanisansa: The Ship of the Serpent-King

region.en: Mid-ocean, a lonely island, and the river road to Benares (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 大洋孤島與歸途河岸（象徵標記）

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: A pious layman so absorbed in thoughts of the Buddha walks dry-foot over a river; in a former life, shipwrecked with a barber on an island, he wins a serpent-king transformed into a jewelled ship -- and by transferring to his companion the whole merit of his virtue, gifts and powers, brings the unholy man aboard too.
summary.zh: 一虔信居士赴祇園途中，心念佛德，雙足踏河竟如履平地，至中流方覺波浪，收攝心神復行。佛陀憶往昔：一持戒弟子與理髮師同船，海中失事，漂流孤島。弟子一心繫念三寶，龍王感其德，化身寶船，海神掌舵。海神只許居士登船，居士遂將己所有布施、持戒、修持之功德悉數轉與理髮師，二人同渡至波羅奈。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: A faithful elect disciple, going to Jetavana at evening, found the ferry pulled up on the bank for service; his mind full of delightful thoughts of the Buddha, he set foot on the river Aciravati -- and his feet did not sink. He reached mid-stream walking as though on dry land; but there he noticed the waves, his ecstasy subsided, and he began to sink. Strung up again to high tension, he walked on over the water to Jetavana, and told the Master. 'You are not the only one,' said the Buddha, 'who has kept safe by remembering the Buddha's virtues,' and told an old-world tale.

In the days of Kassapa Buddha a disciple who had entered on the Paths took ship with a barber of some property, whose wife had given him in charge of the holy man for better and worse. A week later the ship was wrecked in mid-ocean, and the two, clinging to one plank, were cast up on an island. The barber killed some birds and offered a share; 'No, thank you,' said the lay brother, who had eaten nothing -- for he thought, 'In this place there is no help for us except the Three Jewels,' and pondered their blessings over and over.

As he pondered, a Serpent-king born in that isle changed his own body into the shape of a great ship filled with the seven kinds of precious things -- masts of sapphire, anchor of gold, ropes of silver, planks of gold -- with a Spirit of the Sea for helmsman, crying, 'Any passengers for India?' The lay brother went to board and would have called his friend; but the helmsman said, 'You may come, but not he: he is not a man of holy life; I brought this ship for you, not for him.' 'Very well: the gifts I have given, the virtues I have practised, the powers I have developed -- I give him the fruit of all of them!' 'I thank you, master!' said the barber, and both were carried oversea, landed at Benares, and enriched by the spirit's power. 'Behold the fruit of sacrifice, virtue, and piety: a serpent in ship-shape conveys the good man o'er the sea,' sang the Sea-spirit, hovering in mid-air, before it went to its own abode.

title.en: Valahassa: The Flying Horse and the Goblin Women

region.en: The goblin city of Sirisavatthu in Ceylon, reached by shipwrecked merchants (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 師子洲須利沙伐都妖城（象徵標記）

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: Five hundred shipwrecked traders are wedded by goblin wives who, when new castaways appear, bind their old husbands in magic chains and devour them. A magic flying horse cries 'Who wants to go home?' three times over the island; two hundred and fifty climb up or cling to its tail, and those who stay behind are eaten.
summary.zh: 五百商人船破漂至師子洲妖女之城。妖女偽作人婦，誘以飲食恩愛，俟新落難者至，則以魔索縛舊夫於受苦之屋而食之。首商夜覺妖妻身冷如屍，識破詭計。晨起相告，二百五十人願從其言。時菩薩化身神馬，白如雪，越海而來，三呼『誰欲還家』，遂負之攀之，盡載二百五十人還鄉；不從者果為妖女所食。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: On the island of Ceylon stood a goblin town called Sirisavatthu, peopled by she-goblins. When a ship is wrecked they adorn and deck themselves, and taking rice and gruel, with trains of slaves and children on their hips, they come up to the castaways, making them see here and there men ploughing and tending kine, herds and dogs, to persuade them that theirs is a city of human beings. 'Very good, noble sirs; it is three years since our own husbands went aboard ship; you are merchants too -- we will be your wives.' Thus they lead the men by wiles and dalliance into the goblin city; then those caught before are bound with magic chains and cast into the house of torment, while new husbands are found.

Once five hundred shipwrecked traders were brought in this way, five hundred goblins taking five hundred husbands. At night, while her man slept, the chief she-goblin rose and went to the house of death, slew some of the men and ate them, and the others did the same. When she came back her body was cold, and the eldest merchant, embracing her, knew her for a goblin. 'All the five hundred must be goblins! As soon as other shipwrecked men can be found, they will make them their husbands and will eat us: come, let us escape!' Two hundred and fifty answered, 'We cannot leave them: go ye if ye will.' Then the chief trader with his two hundred and fifty fled in fear.

At that time the Bodhisatta had come into the world as a flying horse, white all over, beaked like a crow, possessed of supernatural power. From the Himalaya he flew through the air to Ceylon, and as he passed over the ponds and tanks he thrice uttered human speech filled with mercy: 'Who wants to go home? Who wants to go home?' The traders cried, 'We are going home, master!' and joined their hands in reverence. 'Then climb up on my back.' Some climbed up, some laid hold of his tail, and even those who only stood saluting were lifted up and conveyed, all two hundred and fifty, to their own country, each set down in his own place. But the she-goblins, when other men came to that place, slew those who had stayed behind and devoured them. 'They who hearken to the Buddha when he tells them what to do, as the bird-horse saved the merchants, they shall win salvation too,' said the Master.

title.en: Bandhanagara: The Stronger Fetters

region.en: Benares in the Kasi country, and the Himalaya retreats
region.zh: 迦尸國波羅奈城與喜馬拉雅林居

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: A poor man, meaning to turn hermit, is put off by his wife from one pregnancy to the next and from weaning to weaning; seeing the trap, he flees by night to the Himalayas, and from the rapture of meditation declares that not iron, ropes nor bars of wood can hold as fast as passion and the love of child, wife, and gold.
summary.zh: 窮人欲出家，妻屢以懷孕、哺育為辭挽留。菩薩自知永無脫期，遂於夜間不辭而別。城衛捉之，以贍母之故得釋，終入雪山修行，得禪定五通，自慶道：『妻子之愛、慾望之縛，至難解者，今解矣！』並誦偈言鐵索木杻不如心縛。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: When a gang of burglars, highwaymen and murderers stood bound in chains before the king of Kosala, thirty Brethren on their rounds saw them and asked the Master at evening whether any fetter were stronger than these. 'Those are fetters indeed,' he answered, 'but the fetters of craving -- for wealth, corn, sons, wives and children -- are stronger than they a hundredfold, nay a thousandfold; yet even those fetters have been broken by wise men of the olden time, who went to Himalaya and became anchorites.'

Once at Benares the Bodhisatta was born in a poor man's family, earned wages, and supported his mother. His mother, much against his will, brought a wife home for him, and soon after died. Not knowing that his wife had conceived, the man said, 'Wife, you must earn your living; I will renounce the world.' 'Nay,' said she, 'I am with child: wait and see the child that is born of me, and then go and become a hermit.' He agreed. When she was delivered he said, 'Now, wife, you are safely delivered, and I must turn hermit.' 'Wait,' said she, 'till the child is weaned.' And after that she conceived again.

'If I agree to her request, I shall never get away at all,' thought the Bodhisatta; and he fled without a word in the night. The city guards seized him, but let him go when he said he had a mother to support, and passing out by the chief gate he made his way to the Himalayas, where he dwelt a recluse, causing the Supernatural Faculties and the Attainments to spring up within him. As he dwelt in the rapture of meditation he exulted: 'The bond of wife and child, the bond of passion, so hard to break, is broken!' and sang that not iron fetters, not ropes or bars of wood, so fast can hold as passion and the love of child or wife, of precious gems and earrings of fine gold.

title.en: Viraka: The Crow Who Would Dive

region.en: A marsh-pool in the Kasi country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 迦尸國澤畔一池（象徵標記）

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: In a famine, a land-crow attaches himself to Viraka the Strong, a marsh crow who catches fish and shares them. Fed and fattened, the crow grows proud -- 'he is black, and so am I' -- insists on diving for his own fish, entangles in the weeds, and drowns while his mate returns to Benares weeping.
summary.zh: 迦尸饑荒，烏鴉離城覓食。薩毘多迦烏見韋羅迦澤鴉捕魚，遂投其門下為僕。韋羅迦每以餘魚與之，鴉漸養尊處優，自念『彼黑我亦黑，眼喙足皆同』，恥於受食，執意親自下水捕魚。韋羅迦勸阻不聽。鴉入水，為水草所纏，唯喙尖出水，窒息而亡。其妻聞訊，泣而歸波羅奈。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: When a famine came upon Kasi and men could no longer spare food for crows, the crows left the famine-stricken land for the woods. A crow of Benares named Savitthaka took his lady and settled beside the pool where Viraka the Strong, a marsh crow, lived. Watching Viraka go down into the water, make a meal off some fish, and come up to dry his feathers, Savitthaka thought, 'Plenty of fish are to be had under the wing of that crow; I will become his servant.' Viraka agreed, and from that time Viraka ate enough fish to keep him alive and gave the rest to Savitthaka, who passed what was over to his wife.

After a while pride came into the crow's heart: 'This crow is black, and so am I; in eyes and beak and feet there is no difference between us. I do not want his fish; I will catch my own!' He told Viraka that for the future he would go down into the water himself. 'Good friend,' said Viraka, 'you do not belong to a tribe of crows born to go into water and catch fish. Do not destroy yourself!' But the warning was not taken to heart.

Down went Savitthaka to the pool and into the water; but he could not make his way through the weeds and come out again. There he was, entangled, with only the tip of his beak appearing above the water, and so, unable to breathe, he perished beneath it. His mate, finding he did not return, asked Viraka for news, lamenting her sweet-voiced mate whose neck was like the peacock in its sheen; and Viraka sang that he was not born to dive beneath the wave, but what he could not do he needs must try, so the poor bird found a watery grave, entangled in the weeds and left to die. The lady-crow returned to Benares weeping; Devadatta had been incarnate as Savitthaka, and the Master as Viraka.

title.en: Kurunga-miga: The Antelope, the Woodpecker and the Tortoise
title.zh: 俱盧瀰迦本生：三友救難

region.en: A forest thicket by a lake (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 湖畔林叢（象徵標記）

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: An antelope takes the hunter's snare; the tortoise gnaws the leather thongs while the woodpecker twice strikes the hunter's face as an ill omen to hold him back. When the tortoise is bagged in turn, the antelope feigns weakness, leads the man deep into the forest, doubles back, and rips the bag open with his horns.
summary.zh: 羚羊夜間飲水誤入獵師皮網，大聲呼救。好友啄木鳥與龜聞聲而來，分頭行事：龜以齒齧革索，啄木鳥飛至獵人家門口，待其持刀出門便撞面撲擊，獵人以為凶兆，兩度折返。索齧斷，羚羊遁入林中。然龜力竭就擒，被縛袋中掛於樹。羚羊不忍，故意示弱引獵師深入密林，繞道疾返，以角挑袋，救出龜。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: Once when Brahmadatta reigned in Benares, the Bodhisatta was an antelope living in a thicket near a lake, in friendship with a woodpecker perched in a tree-top and a tortoise in the water. A hunter, wandering in the wood, observed the antelope's track at the going down to the water, and set a snare of leather strong as an iron chain. In the first watch of the night the antelope went down to drink and was caught, and cried loud and long.

The woodpecker flew down from her tree-top and the tortoise came out of the water, and they consulted. 'Friend, you have teeth -- bite this snare through; I will see to it that the hunter keeps away,' said the woodpecker. At dawn the hunter came out knife in hand; the bird uttered a cry, flapped his wings and struck him in the face. 'Some bird of ill omen has struck me!' thought the hunter, and turned back to lie down. He rose again and left by the back door -- but the bird had reasoned the same way and struck him again. Not till sunrise did he dare go out.

By then the tortoise had gnawed through all the thongs but one, his mouth smeared with blood and his teeth as if about to fall out; the antelope burst the last thong and fled into the woods, while the exhausted tortoise lay where he was and was bagged and hung on a tree. Seeing his friend taken, the antelope determined to save him: he let the hunter see him, made as though weak, and kept just out of reach, leading the man deep into the forest; then he gave him the slip and returned swift as the wind by another way, lifted the bag with his horns, ripped it open and let the tortoise out. Then he warned them both -- the woodpecker to migrate with her brood, the tortoise to dive into the water -- and the three friends lived all their lives in unbroken amity.

title.en: Sumsumara: The Monkey and the Crocodile

region.en: A forest bend of the Ganges below the Himalaya (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 雪山之下恆河灣林（象徵標記）

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: A crocodile's mate cravings the monkey-king's heart to eat; the crocodile carries his passenger into mid-stream and confesses the design, only to be told that monkeys keep their hearts in fig-trees -- and made to ferry his quarry back to shore with heart intact and wits smaller.
summary.zh: 鱷魚之妻貪求猴王之心以為食。鱷魚誘猴登背，游至中流潛水，直言欲取其心。猴王急中生智：『若心在身中，跳躍樹梢早已碎矣；心懸於彼岸無花果樹上。』鱷魚信之，載猴返岸。猴跳上樹後訕笑之：『身軀雖大，智實渺小。』

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Bodhisatta came to life as a monkey, strong and sturdy, living by a curve of the river Ganges in a forest haunt below the Himalaya. A crocodile dwelt in the Ganges, and his mate, seeing the monkey's great frame, conceived a longing to eat his heart. 'Good wife,' said the crocodile, 'I live in the water and he lives on dry land: how can we catch him?' 'By hook or by crook, caught he must be: if I do not get him, I shall die.'

When the monkey sat on the bank after drinking, the crocodile drew near: 'Why do you live on bad fruits in this old place? Across the Ganges the mango trees are endless, with fruit sweet as honey. Better cross over.' 'Deep and wide is the Ganges; how shall I get across?' 'Mount on my back and I will carry you.' The monkey trusted him and climbed up; but when they had swum a little way, the crocodile plunged his passenger under the water.

'Good friend, you are letting me sink!' cried the monkey. 'What is that for?' 'You think I carry you out of pure good nature? My wife has a longing for your heart, and I want to give it her to eat.' 'Friend, it is nice of you to tell me. If our heart were inside us when we go jumping among the tree-tops, it would be all knocked to pieces -- we keep it hanging on yonder fig-tree.' 'Show me your heart and I will not kill you.' The crocodile brought him to the tree; the monkey leapt off, climbed up and sat laughing: 'O silly crocodile! You thought there were creatures that kept their hearts in a tree-top! Great is your body, but how much smaller is your wit! Now go your ways, for I have had the best of it.' The crocodile, feeling as sad as if he had lost a thousand pieces of money, went back sorrowing.

title.en: Ucchittha-bhatta: Hot Above, Cold Below

region.en: A village in the Kasi country
region.zh: 迦尸國一村

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: A begging tumbler, kept waiting while a lover dines on the goodman's rice, is served the leftovers hot on top and cold beneath, and tells the returned husband where the man is hidden -- then, to a lovesick Brother hankering after the same woman, the Master reveals that she once made him eat another man's leavings.
summary.zh: 一乞食者立於門前待施，婆羅門之妻正與情人共餐。夫歸，情人匿於庫房，妻以熱飯覆於其殘飯之上。乞者探之，上熱下冷，心知有異，遂為丈夫一一說破，並從庫房中揪出其人。佛陀以此誡一思念亡妻之比丘：此婦昔曾使汝食他人之餘飯。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: Once at a village in Kasi there was a brahmin whose wife was bad and wicked and did wrong. One day, while her husband was abroad, her lover came; she served him rice hot with sauce and curry, and stood at the door watching for the brahmin's coming, while a begging tumbler, one of a poor family of acrobats, stood waiting at the door for a morsel.

When the husband drew nigh, she ran in quickly and made her lover go down into the store-room; then she gave her husband a seat and water for washing, and upon the cold rice the other had left she turned out some hot rice. The brahmin put his hand in and felt it hot above and cold below. 'This must be some one else's leavings,' he thought, and asked the reason. Again and again he asked, but she, fearing discovery, held her peace.

Then a thought came into the tumbler's mind: 'The man down in the store-room must be a lover, and this is the master of the house. Soho! I will declare the whole matter.' He told the brahmin everything -- how, when he had gone out, another had come in and done evil, how the rice had been eaten first, and the man was hidden in the store-room -- and repeated his stanza, hot at top and cold at bottom, and I am a tumbler, sir; the man you seek is hiding in the store-room. By his top-knot the brahmin hauled the man out, bade him take care not to do the like again, and gave both wife and lover such a lesson that they were not likely to repeat it. And the Master told the lovesick Brother that his late wife was that lady, and that this same woman in former days had made him eat the leavings of her paramour.

title.en: Kuta-vanija: The Judge and the Mice That Ate Iron

region.en: The court of justice at Benares in the Kasi country
region.zh: 迦尸國波羅奈城法庭

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: A cheat who swears that mice ate his friend's five hundred deposited ploughshares hears his own son accused of being carried off by a hawk; the Lord Justice accepts the parallel, and the ploughshares and the boy come home together.
summary.zh: 村商以五百鐵犁寄存城商處，城商變賣得錢，撒鼠糧於地，謊稱犁為鼠所食。村商趁其子沐浴之機藏之，詐稱孩子被鷹抓走。二人對簿公堂，菩薩判官問：『鷹能抓走孩童乎？』城商理直氣壯反問：『若鷹不能抓孩童，鼠豈能食鐵犁？』判官撫掌曰『以其人之道還治其人之身』，判還犁與子。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: Two traders of Savatthi, one pious and one a cheat, journeyed east and west with five hundred waggons and returned with large profits. In a story of the past, when Brahmadatta reigned in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a Lord Justice, and two traders, one from a village and one of the town, were friends together. The villager deposited five hundred ploughshares with the townsman, who sold them, kept the price, and strewed mouse-dung where they had lain. 'The mice have eaten them up,' he said, and pointed to the droppings.

'Well, well, so be it,' said the villager. 'What can be done with things which the mice have eaten?' But at bathing time he took the cheat's son to a friend's house, set him in an inner chamber, and went to bathe himself. 'Where is my son?' asked the cheat. 'Dear friend, I took him with me to the river; when I was gone down into the water, there came a hawk, seized your son in his extended claws and flew up into the air. I beat the water and shouted, but could not make him let go.' 'Lies! No hawk could carry off a boy. I will have you dragged before the judge!' 'As you please.'

Before the Bodhisatta the cheat stated his case, and the villager calmly replied: 'My lord, if hawks cannot carry off boys into the air, can mice eat iron ploughshares? This man says the mice ate my ploughshares; give sentence whether they are eaten or no. Judge my cause!' 'He must have meant to fight the trickster with his own weapons,' thought the judge, and sang: Well planned indeed! The biter bit, the trickster tricked -- a pretty hit! If mice eat ploughshares, hawks can fly with boys away into the sky. Thus he that lost his son received him again, and he received his ploughshares that had lost them.

title.en: Dhammaddhaja: The Impossible Tasks

region.en: The royal court and park of Benares in the Kasi country
region.zh: 迦尸國波羅奈王庭與御苑

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: Losing his bribes to a chaplain who judges justly, Commander Kalaka works the king into demanding a garden, a jewel lake, an ivory house and a light-giving jewel overnight -- which Sakka, palace grown hot with pity, supplies. The last task, a park-keeper endowed with four virtues, defeats even a god, until Sakka names the humble ornament-maker who actually possesses them, and the mob stones the slanderer.
summary.zh: 統帥迦羅卡因受賄之路被斷，向王進讒。國王命師菩薩一夜造園，又造七寶湖、象牙宮殿、放光寶珠——帝釋天宮發熱，親為造之。末題：造一位具四德之守園人。薩凱自承神亦不能造，卻指點明臣：國中首飾匠查達巴尼正具此四德。四德之源一一自陳，眾怒而擊殺迦羅卡。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: A king of Benares, named Yasapani the Glorious, was a good king; but his chief captain Kalaka swallowed bribes in judging causes and defrauded the rightful owners. When the Bodhisatta, the king's chaplain Dhammaddhaja, reversed one of the captain's unjust sentences to the applause of all, the king made the chaplain a judge; and Kalaka, losing his gains, slandered him as a coveter of the kingdom. To work his death, he advised the king to demand impossibilities.

'Make us a garden to disport ourselves in tomorrow -- if you cannot, you must die.' The Bodhisatta went home, ate, and lay down to think; and Sakka's palace grew hot, for such is the sign when a good man is in straits. Sakka hastened to him and made a garden like the groves of Nandana, with fence of eighteen cubits, gates and ponds, heavy with flowers and fruit. Then a lake with a hundred landing-places, covered with lotuses of five colours; then a house all of ivory; then a jewel to light the king's walks -- each provided overnight by Sakka, each announced by Kalaka as proof that the sage could seize the kingdom.

Last, 'not even a deity can make a man with all four virtues; bid him make a keeper with these four.' The Bodhisatta reasoned that what Sakka could make, he had made, but such a man could not be made even by a god; better to die forlorn in the woods than by the hand of men. Sitting beneath a tree in the forest he was found by Sakka in a forester's shape, and confessed his resolve. Then Sakka declared himself: 'I made the park and all the rest; a keeper with four virtues cannot be made -- but in your country Chattapani, maker of ornaments for the head, is such a man.'

Brought before the king, Chattapani owned the four virtues: he envied not, since a woman once made him cast a learned chaplain into bonds and the man's teaching freed his envy; he drank no wine, since once, mad with drink, he wrung his own son's neck and ate his flesh unknowing; he had no strong desires, since a son's death through insolence to a Pacceka Buddha taught him the vanity of affection; and he knew no wrath, since seven years of charity as King Araka had won him seven ages in Brahma's heaven. The whole court rose upon Kalaka, broke his head and cast him on a dunghill, and the king thenceforward ruled in righteousness.

title.en: Cula-nandiya: The Monkeys Who Gave Their Lives

region.en: The Himalaya forests, and a banyan-tree of the border-land (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喜馬拉雅山林與邊地一榕樹（象徵標記）

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: Two monkey brothers leave their herd to feed a blind mother; when a cruel huntsman raises his bow at her, first one brother then the other offers his own life for hers -- while at the huntsman's own home a thunderbolt burns wife and children, and the earth opens beneath his feet.
summary.zh: 二猴為盲母棄群而居邊地榕樹，日日採果飼母。一獵師受業師誡『勿行惡』而不悟，獵歸空手，見樹上老猴，舉弓欲射。兄歡喜躍下：『勿傷吾母，我願代死！』弟歡喜兒亦然。獵師盡殺母子三猴。歸家則天雷燒其妻子屋舍，行至村口梁柱斷落碎顱，地裂獄火吞噬。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: When Brahmadatta reigned in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a monkey named Nandiya, or Jolly, and his youngest brother Jollikin; together they led a band of eighty thousand monkeys and had a blind mother to care for. They left her in her lair and went amongst the trees for sweet wild fruit, sending it home by messengers who never delivered it, till she was nothing but skin and bone. Then both brothers left the herd, brought their mother down out of Himalaya, and took up their abode in a banyan-tree of the border-land to care for her.

A brahmin of Takkasila had been warned by his teacher, who read harshness in his lineaments: 'Be not harsh, nor do what you will afterwards repent.' The youth married and settled in Benares, and lived by his bow as a huntsman. Returning empty-handed one day, he saw the banyan on the verge of an open glade; the two brothers had just fed their mother and sat behind her in the branches. Seeing the mother weak with age and blind, the huntsman lifted his bow to shoot her.

The Bodhisatta cried, 'O man, don't shoot my mother! She is blind and weak for age. I will save her life -- don't kill her, but kill me instead!' He came down and sat within bowshot, and the huntsman shot him dead; then prepared to shoot the mother. Jollikin came down: 'Even if she only lives a day, she will have received the gift of life. Take both us brothers and spare our mother!' He too was shot, and the mother after; all three hung on the carrying-pole. At that moment a thunderbolt fell on the wicked man's house and burnt his wife and two children with it. Told at the village gate, he dropped his load, threw off his garments and ran homewards naked, wailing; the bamboo uprights broke and fell upon his head and crushed it, the earth yawned, flame rose from hell, and as he was swallowed up he remembered his master's warning: whatever a man does, the same he in himself will find; our deeds are all like seeds and bring forth fruit in kind.

title.en: Sabbadatha: The Jackal Who Stole a Spell
title.zh: 薩婆達多本生：竊咒胡狼

region.en: The royal park and city gates of Benares in the Kasi country
region.zh: 迦尸國波羅奈王苑與城門

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: A jackal lying in a hole overhears a brahmin reciting the spell of subduing the world, learns it better than its owner, and raises all fourfooted creatures under the title All-tusk. Besieging Benares he is dared to make the very lion he sits on roar; the roar terrifies the elephants, and the pretender is trampled to atoms -- while the first drying of meat dates from that day.
summary.zh: 胡狼竊聽婆羅門誦『降世咒』，自誇更勝其主。誦咒召來數百胡狼，繼而象馬獅虎豬鹿盡集帳下，自號『薩婆達多』（全牙），騎於獅上、獅立於二象之背。揮軍十二由旬圍波羅奈。菩薩國師令城中人皆以麵粉塞耳，再登樓挑戰：『爾敢令身下之獅一吼乎？』胡狼以足叩獅，獅三吼，象嚇墜胡狼，踐之成泥；群獸自相驚撞而亡，積屍十二由旬。傳說肉乾之製始於此日。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: A chaplain of the king of Benares knew the spell entitled Of Subduing the World, which could be taught to no one without a special rite; reciting it once on a flat stone in a place apart, he little knew that a jackal lying in a hole got it by heart -- for the jackal had been a brahmin who learned the same spell in a former existence. 'Ho, brahmin! I have learnt the spell better than you know it yourself!' cried the jackal, and made off into the forest.

There the jackal found a she-jackal, repeated the spell, and had some hundreds of jackals under his orders; then he gathered round him all the elephants and horses, lions and tigers, swine and deer, and all other fourfooted creatures, and became their king under the title of Sabbadatha, All-tusk. On the back of two elephants stood a lion, and on the lion's back sat Sabbadatha with his she-jackal consort, and great honour was paid them. Puffed up with pride, he marched a host covering twelve leagues to the walls of Benares and sent the king a message: give up your kingdom, or fight for it.

The terrified citizens shut their gates; but the chaplain said, 'Fear not: leave the jackal to me,' and made proclamation by beat of drum that every dweller in Benares over all its twelve leagues must stop up his ears with flour -- and their cats and other animals too. From the gate-tower he called, 'Sabbadatha, what will you do to take this realm?' 'I will cause the lions to roar and frighten the multitude.' 'These noble lions will never do the bidding of an old jackal like you!' 'I will make even this one, upon whose back I sit, roar alone!' And he tapped with his foot: the lion, resting his mouth on the elephant's temple, roared thrice without stay. The elephants dropped the jackal at their feet and trampled his head to atoms; then, hearing the roar, they wounded one another and perished, and the rest of the creatures perished too, all except the lions, which fled to the woods. The chaplain had the gates thrown open and proclaimed: let the people take the flour from their ears, and let those who desire meat take it -- and so, tradition says, men first began to dry meat.

title.en: Guttila: The Musician and His Rival Pupil
title.zh: 瞿提羅本生：琴師與逆徒

region.en: Benares in the Kasi country, and the city of the gods (the heaven scenes are a symbolic pin)
region.zh: 迦尸國波羅奈城與天界（天界部分為象徵標記）

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: Master Guttila, forced by his blind parents to teach a scurvy pupil, is challenged to a contest before all Benares. Sakka coaches him -- break every string, and the body of the lute will fill twelve leagues with music -- and nine hundred dancing nymphs crown the old master's triumph; a week in heaven questioning the nymphs on their merits sends him home resolved on generosity.
summary.zh: 琴師瞿提羅為全印度之冠，奉養盲親。優闍尼商人嫌其地樂師默西拉之技，默西拉遂求學於瞿提羅。師察其非善人，父母再三哀求方允。學成，默西拉索同等俸祿，與師約期七日較技。老師自慮技窮，六日間逃於林中，草死徑成。帝釋座熱，現身許諾：斷一弦，聲如故；斷七弦，以身作琴，聲滿十二由旬；擲骰則天女下舞。比賽之日，默西拉弦斷無聲，為眾人亂棒打死。瞿提羅受帝釋之邀，昇天七日，問三十七位天女生前何德所致，歸而告民，人皆發心行善。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: Master Guttila of Benares, chief of all the musicians in India, married no wife but maintained his blind parents. Traders from Ujjeni, knowing his music, scorned their own chief player Musila as sounding like scratching on a mat or women crooning to soothe their babies; Musila gave back his hire and begged to be taken to Benares. There he tuned and played Guttila's lute till the blind old parents cried, 'The mice are gnawing at the lute!' -- and then begged to be taught. The Bodhisatta, skilled in divining from lineaments, saw he was not a good man and refused; but the parents besought him again and again, till he yielded.

He stinted nothing, and taught his pupil all he knew. 'Your knowledge is now perfect,' said he. But Musila schemed to stay in the chief city of India and serve the king on equal terms; the king, told of it, offered him the half of Guttila's fee. 'If I receive the same as you, I will serve; if not, not -- do I not know all that you know?' The king set a contest for the seventh day, and beat the drum round the city. Guttila thought, 'If my pupil beats me, death in the woods is better than the shame,' and for six days fled to the woods and returned, till the grass died and his feet wore a path.

Sakka's throne grew hot, and he came to the master: 'Fear not, for I will help thee at thy need.' As you play, break one string and play upon six; Musila shall break a string and make no more music. Then break the second, the third, even to the seventh, and go on playing on the body alone; the sound shall fill all the land of Benares for twelve leagues. And when you have thrown my three dice in the air, three hundred nymphs shall descend and dance at each throw, and I will come with them. At the contest Guttila's broken strings gave out a music divine while Musila's was dumb; nine hundred nymphs danced before the king, and the multitude, crying that Musila had not known his measure, beat and bruised him to death and cast him on a dustheap.

Sakka then sent Matali with the divine car to fetch Guttila to heaven, where the daughters of the gods begged to hear him play for seven days. He asked in return what deeds of merit had brought each thither: one had given an upper garment to a Brother in the time of Buddha Kassapa, another flowers, another a five-spray wreath, another sweet fruits; one had heard the discourse of Brethren; one had stood in the water giving water to a Brother; one had done her duty by her parents-in-law without losing her temper. 'Tis good for me that I came here and heard by how small a merit great glory is attained,' said Guttila; and when he was sent home to Benares he told the people what he had seen, and from that time the people resolved to do good deeds with all their might.

title.en: Mulapariyaya: 'Time All Consumes'
title.zh: 根本法門本生：孰吞時間

region.en: The Subhaga park at Ukkattha, and Benares in the story of the past (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 憍薩羅欝伽陀伽喜樂園與過去世的波羅奈城（象徵標記）

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: Five hundred pupils, certain that they know all their master knows, tap the jujube tree in mockery; he asks them who consumes the all-consuming, they cannot answer in seven days, and are humbled -- as the Buddha later humbled five hundred brahmins drunk with pride by repeating the Chapter on the Succession of Causes.
summary.zh: 五百弟子自以為所學已盡，譏師為『無用之樹』。菩薩問：『時間吞食一切，連時間本身亦被吞食，孰吞食此吞食一切者？』七日無解，眾愧而歸順。佛陀在欝伽陀伽林為五百驕慢婆羅門誦〈相續經〉，彼等一字不解，慚伏如無牙之蛇。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: Five hundred brahmins who had mastered the Three Vedas embraced salvation and studied the Three Pitakas, then grew intoxicated with pride: 'The Supreme Buddha knows just the Three Pitakas, and we know them too; what is the difference between us?' They went about with a following of their own, till the Master repeated before them the Chapter on the Succession of Causes adorned with the Eight Stages of Knowledge -- and they did not understand a word, but became as quiet as serpents with their fangs extracted.

'This is not the first time,' said the Master, 'that I have humbled men who carried their heads so high.' Once at Benares the Bodhisatta, a far-famed teacher, instructed five hundred pupils in sacred verses; they perfected their learning and said, 'We know as much as our teacher: there is no difference,' and would not come before his face nor do their round of duty. One day, seeing their master seated beneath a jujube tree, they tapped it with their fingers: 'A worthless tree!' The Bodhisatta observed the mockery and said, 'My pupils, I will ask you a question,' and repeated: Time all consumes, even time itself as well; who is it consumes the all-consumer? -- tell!

Not one of the youths could answer. 'Do not imagine this question is in the Three Vedas. You imagine you know all that I know, and so you act like the jujube tree: you do not know that I know a great deal unknown to you. I give you seven days.' For a week they pondered and could make neither head nor tail of it. On the seventh day they came and confessed; and the teacher rebuked them -- heads grow on necks, and hair on heads will grow: how many heads have ears, I wish to know? -- solved the problem, and was forgiven. They quenched their pride and waited upon the Bodhisatta.

title.en: Suka: The Parrot Who Slept on the Wing

region.en: The Himalaya skirts, and a mango island beyond the sea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喜馬拉雅山麓與海外芒果島（象徵標記）

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: A parrot-son flies daily over the sea to a golden mango island for his blind old parents, until his father warns him parrots that go thither have not length of life. Disobeying, he gorges, sleeps in mid-flight, drops mango and all, and a fish ends the errand -- as the Buddha recalls to a Brother who died of over-eating.
summary.zh: 老鸚鵡王目盲，其子日日飛越大海往金芒島取果供親。父警之曰：往彼島之鸚鵡皆不得長壽，勿再往。子不聽。一日貪食過量，銜芒歸途，倦極而眠，果墜水，身亦沉，為魚所吞。父母失供而亡。佛陀以此誡一飽食致死的比丘。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: When king Brahmadatta reigned over Benares, the Bodhisatta was a parrot, king over several thousands of his kind on the seaward side of the Himalayas, with one son. When the son grew strong the father's eyes grew weak -- for parrots fly with great swiftness, and in age the eye weakens first -- and the young parrot kept his parents in the nest and brought them food.

One day, seeking food, he alighted on a mountain-top, looked over the ocean, and beheld an island with a mango grove full of sweet golden fruit. Thenceforward he flew over each day, sucked the mango juice and carried fruit home. His father, tasting it, knew the island and named it. 'Parrots that go thither, my son, have not length of life: go not to that island again!' But the son obeyed him not, and went yet again.

One day he drank much of the mango juice, and with a mango in his beak was passing over the ocean when, worn out with so long a carrying, sleep mastered him: sleeping he flew on, the fruit fell from his beak, and by degrees he left his path, skimmed the surface and fell in, where a fish caught and devoured him. When he did not return the parents, receiving no sustenance, pined away and died. The Master sang: what time the bird without excess did eat, he found the way and brought his mother meat; but once he ate too much, forgot the mean, he fell, and afterward was seen no more. So be not greedy; modest be in all; to spare is safe, greed goeth before a fall.

title.en: Jarudapana: The Old Treasure Well

region.en: A disused well on the caravan road out of Benares (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波羅奈城外商道上的一口廢井（象徵標記）

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: Traders who dig in an old well for water strike layers of treasure from iron to lapis lazuli, and will not stop; the serpent-king's breath slays the greedy, loads the cart of the one merchant who was content, and sees him home to Benares and a life of giving.
summary.zh: 一行商隊於廢井掘水，得鐵、銅、金、珠寶等層層礦藏。菩薩誡曰：貪為毀滅之根，得此足矣，勿再掘。眾人愈掘愈深，觸怒龍王，以鼻息毒氣盡殺之；唯菩薩得免。龍王親為其套車裝寶，命小龍駕車送歸波羅奈。菩薩散盡珍寶行大布施，命終生天。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: Traders of Savatthi, setting out with laden carts, found a disused well on a difficult part of their road, saw no water, and resolved to dig deeper. As they dug they came upon successive layers of minerals, from iron to lapis lazuli; content, they filled their waggons with the treasure and returned safe to Savatthi, where they gave food to the Brotherhood in thanksgiving. When they told the Master of the find, he said they had accepted their wealth with all moderation -- 'but in other days there were men not content, who refused to do as wise men advised them, and so lost their lives.'

Once at Benares the Bodhisatta, a great merchant, came with a large caravan to that very wood and that very well. The traders, wanting water, dug, and came upon a quantity of metal and gems; but though they got a great deal, they were discontented. 'There must be another treasure here, better than this!' and they dug and dug. 'Merchants, greed is the root of destruction,' said the Bodhisatta. 'You have won a great deal of wealth; with this be content, and dig no more.' But they dug the more.

Now the well was haunted by serpents. The Serpent-king, incensed at the falling of clods and earth, slew the greedy diggers with the breath of his nostrils, all saving the Bodhisatta; then he came up from the serpent world, put the oxen to the carts, filled them with jewels, seated the Bodhisatta on a fine waggon, made certain young serpents drive the carts, and brought him to Benares, setting the treasure in order in his house. The Bodhisatta spent the treasure so that he made much stir throughout all India by his almsgiving, and, keeping the deeds of virtue and the holy days, came at his life's end to paradise.

title.en: Maha-panada: The Palace Under the Ganges
title.zh: 大波那陀本生：水底王宮

region.en: The Ganges below the village of Koti (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 拘帝村下之恆河（象徵標記）

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: Elder Bhaddaji, a magnificent young convert who entered sainthood during a meal, is pressed mid-river by the Master to say where he lived when Great Panada was king: 'Here, under the water.' Lifting the whole hundred-storeyed palace of his former life on one finger, he rises into the air to silence doubting monks -- then drops it back when his fish-and-turtle kinsfolk tumble out.
summary.zh: 富商之子跋陀吉豪奢冠世，聞法證果，剃度為僧。佛陀與之同船渡恆河，中流問曰：『汝為大波那陀王時，宮殿安在？』答曰：『在此水底。』長老以神通力一指舉起整座百層寶宮，凌空三由旬，眾疑頓釋。然昔為宮中魚鱉蛇蛙之親眷聞聲竄出，佛陀提醒，長老遂還宮於水。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: When the Master had passed the rains at Savatthi he travelled to Bhaddiya to show kindness to young Bhaddaji, the only son of a rich merchant with three season-houses and a fortune of eight hundred millions, whose progress through the town was the wonder of all. But on the day of the Master's departure the streets were empty: the whole town was listening to his discourse. Bhaddaji heard it too, threw off all his sins, and attained to high fruition and sainthood; and when his father was told the young man might enter Nirvana that very day, he begged first for his ordination.

On alms-pilgrimage with the Master, Bhaddaji sat in trance by a landing-place of the Ganges at the village of Koti, rising for none but the Master -- which made the unconverted folk angry. When rafts were built the Master called him aboard, and in mid-river asked: 'Bhaddaji, where is the palace you lived in when Great Panada was king?' 'Here, under the water,' was the reply. The doubters murmured that the Elder was showing himself a saint.

Then Bhaddaji, bowing to his Master, took the whole pile of the palace on one finger by his mysterious power and rose in the air bearing it with him -- it covered a space of twenty-five leagues. He tossed the building above the water first one league, then two, then three; and those who had been his kinsfolk in that former existence, now come to life as fish, tortoises, water-snakes and frogs because they loved the palace so much, wriggled out and tumbled over and over into the water again. 'Bhaddaji, your relations are in trouble,' said the Master, and the Elder let the palace go, and it sank to the place where it had been. The Master repeated the old king's verses: 'Twas king Panada who this palace had, a thousand bowshots high, in breadth sixteen; an hundred storeys, all of emerald green.

title.en: Uluka: The Owl That Was Not Crowned

region.en: A flat rock in the Himalayas where the birds met (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喜馬拉雅山中鳥會之磐石（象徵標記）

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: In the world's first age men, beasts, fish and birds each choose a king; the birds pick the owl, and proclamation is made twice. On the third announcement a crow rises to object -- 'if this is his face in good humour, what when angry?' -- and flies off cawing his dissent, beginning the feud of crows and owls.
summary.zh: 初劫之時，人立王，獸立獅，魚立阿難，唯鳥無王。眾鳥集於磐石，選鴞為王，傳令三遍。第三遍時一鴉起而抗聲：『加冕之時尚作此態，震怒之時當如何？如芝麻撒於熱釜！』遂飛翔空中，連呼『吾不奉詔』。鴞起身追之，自此鴉鴞結仇。眾鳥改立金鵝為王。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: When a Brother sweeping his cell found a basketful of crows' heads dropped from the trees by owls, the Brethren asked how long the crows and owls had been at enmity. 'Since the time of the first age of the world,' said the Master, and told an old-world tale.

In the first cycle of the world the people gathered and took for their king a man handsome, auspicious and commanding; the quadrupeds chose the Lion, and the fish of the ocean chose a fish called Ananda. Then all the birds in the Himalayas assembled upon a flat rock: 'Among men there is a king, and among the beasts, and the fish have one too; we should not live in anarchy. Fix on some one fit to be set in the king's place!' They searched about and chose the Owl, and a bird made proclamation three times that a vote would be taken on the matter.

After patiently hearing the announcement twice, on the third time up rose a Crow: 'Stay now! If that is what he looks like when he is being consecrated king, what will he look like when he is angry? If he only looks at us in anger, we shall be scattered like sesame seeds thrown on a hot plate. I do not want to make this fellow king!' Granted leave to speak his mind, he enlarged upon it: 'I like not, with all deference be it said, to have the Owl anointed as our head; look at his face! if this good humour be, what will he do when he looks angrily?' Then he flew up into the air, cawing 'I don't like it! I don't like it!' The Owl rose and pursued him; thenceforward those two nursed enmity one towards another. And the birds chose a golden Goose for their king and dispersed.

title.en: Kurudhamma: The Righteousness of the Kurus

region.en: Indapatta city in the Kuru kingdom, and drought-stricken Dantapura in Kalinga (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 俱盧國因陀羅巴陀城與迦陵伽但陀補羅城（象徵標記）

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: Drought-stricken Kalinga asks the righteous Kuru king for his state elephant; rain still fails, so the Kalinga king sends for the very Five Virtues themselves -- collected, scruple by scruple, from eleven lay figures who each fear the smallest stain, down to a courtesan whom Sakka himself tested. Written on a golden plate, the precepts bring rain to Kalinga at last.
summary.zh: 迦陵伽大旱，民人號泣。國王臥草蓆七日求雨不得。聞俱盧國行五戒故雨水時至，先求其寶象，得之而雨不至；復遣婆羅門求『俱盧正法』。王、母、王后、副王、國師、御者、車伕、富商、倉吏、守門人、妓女，皆以纖介之疑自陳其心——如誤踏蟹穴、誤以妹為婦等——眾人皆曰：『非意之罪，不入於帳。』逐一書於金版。國王習之，迦陵伽雨澤遂降。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: A Brother who could shoot a pebble through a wild goose's eye was rebuked by the Master, who told of the Kuru righteousness. Once Dhananjaya reigned at Indapatta in the Kuru kingdom, and the Bodhisatta his son, grown king, kept the ten royal duties and the Five Virtues -- as did queen-mother, queen-consort, viceroy, family priest, driver, courtier, charioteer, treasurer, master of the granaries, noble, porter, courtesan and slave-girl, every one. He built six almonries and daily distributed six hundred thousand pieces in alms, till all India was overspread by his bounty.

In Dantapura of Kalinga, King Kalinga's realm was afflicted: no rain fell, the crops failed, famine stalked the land, and three fears were ever present. Told that former monarchs lay seven days on a grass pallet after alms and vows, the king did so -- and still no rain. 'In Indapatta there is a state elephant, Anjana-vasabho the Black Bull,' said his court. 'The king there loves giving: were he but asked, he would give it without fail.' Eight brahmins went and hailed the Bodhisatta on the road to his almshouse; he examined the elephant three times round for any spot unadorned, besprinkled him with scented water, and made him over with his golden chain, driver and all -- 'a king's portion, worthy of a king.'

But although the elephant was come, no rain fell. 'Your king observes the Kuru righteousness,' said the brahmins on their return; 'our king is wishful himself to observe it: write it on a golden plate and bring it hither.' 'Indeed I did once observe it; but now I am in doubt about this very point. At the Kattika feast I shot a flower-wreathed arrow over the lake, and whether it fell upon some fish I know not; the doubt of life-taking makes a flaw in my virtue. But my mother keeps it well: get it from her.' So it went on: the queen-mother doubted her partiality in dividing sandal-wood and a golden neckband between her daughters-in-law; the queen at her lattice had looked with love upon the viceroy; the viceroy had let a crowd stand all night in the wet; the chaplain had coveted a sun-bright chariot; the driver's measuring-stick had perchance crushed a crab in its hole; the charioteer's goad had tired the steeds; the rich man had tied a handful of untithed rice; the granary-master's markers had perchance fallen on the measured heap; the porter had called a woodman's sister his wife.

Each time the messengers answered: 'What is done without intent is not counted to the score. If you feel a scruple in so small a matter, what real transgression could you ever commit?' And from each they received the Five Virtues -- Slay not the living; take not what is not given; walk not evilly in lust; speak no lies; drink no strong drink. Last, the courtesan told how Sakka, in the shape of a youth, had given her a thousand pieces and never returned for three years, till she grew so poor she must apply to the Chief Justices for her old wage -- and how at the very moment her hand went out for another man's thousand, Sakka showed himself in his own shape, shining like the sun fresh risen, and filled her dwelling with jewels of seven kinds. 'Merely to hold out the hand is not a breach of virtue: that virtue of yours is the highest perfection!' Thus they bore the golden plate to Dantapura; the Kalinga king practised the Five Virtues, and in all the realm of Kalinga the rain fell, the three fears were allayed, and the land became prosperous and fertile.

title.en: Vaddhaki-sukara: The Carpenter's Boar

region.en: The forests and hills beyond Benares in the Kasi country
region.zh: 迦尸國波羅奈城外山林

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: Reared by carpenters and released into the forest, a tusked boar finds a paradise cave held in terror by one tiger. He arrays the herd in a lotus battle-order, lets the sham hermit's advice lure the tiger into a pit-trap, gores him, then fells the fig-tree under the fleeing hermit with one tusk-blow -- and is consecrated king of the boars on a chair of fig-wood.
summary.zh: 木匠所養之豬牙彎體壯，力能翻樹遞斧，恐為人食，縱之入山。得一石窟，水草豐美，然群豬皆瘦——晨有虎至，見者即被攫。木匠豬夜夜操練，布蓮花陣：母豬幼崽居中，戰豬環外；鑿圓坑陷阱。虎至，群豬不逃，虎作何狀，豬亦作何狀。虎回洞，偽沙門（分食虎祿者）譏其無勇，慫恿再往。虎撲，豬急閃身墮入圓坑之旁小洞，虎墮深坑，豬跳起以牙貫其股，傷其腎而斃之。偽沙門欲逃，爬上榕樹，母豬擔水、幼豬掘根、牙豬撞根，一擊樹倒，眾豬齧其骨。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: Carpenters settled near Benares found a young boar fallen in a pit and kept him; he grew big with curved tusks and well-mannered, turning trees over with his snout and fetching hatchet and adze, chisel and mallet, and pulling the measuring line by the end. Afraid someone might eat him, the carpenter let him go in the forest. The boar found a great cave in a mountain side, with plenty of bulbs and roots and fruits, and some hundreds of boars approached him: 'A nice place it certainly is, but dangerous -- there is a tiger comes in the morning, and every one he sees he seizes and carries off.'

'One alone too many for all of you! I'll catch him, if you only do what I tell you.' At night he drilled the boars and prepared them for war, explaining that war is of three kinds, the lotus army, the wheel army, and the waggon army, and arraying them after the lotus pattern: the mothers and their suckling brood in the middle, then the sows without young, the little boars, the yearlings, the tusked, and the strong battle-boars by tens and twenties in serried ranks. Before his own position he had a round hole dug, and behind it a pit growing gradually deeper, shaped like a winnowing basket.

At dawn the tiger came, stopped upon the plateau, and glared; and at a signal all the boars glared back. Whatever the tiger did, the boars did after him. 'They used to take to their heels as soon as they saw me -- now they stand up against me!' marvelled the tiger, and turned back to his lair. But the sham hermit who shared the tiger's prey mocked his empty paws and urged one roar and one leap; so the tiger plucked up courage and leapt upon the Carpenter's Boar. The boar dodged and dropped into the round hole; the tiger could not stop, but tumbled headlong into the jaws of the deeper pit; up jumped the boar, ran his tusk into the tiger's thighs, tore him about the kidneys and tossed him out of the pit crying, 'Here's your enemy for you!' They who came first had tiger to eat; those who came after went about sniffing at others' mouths, asking what tiger's flesh tasted like.

Still the boars were uneasy: 'the sham hermit can bring ten tigers more!' So they all set forth, found the man, chased him up a fig-tree, and the leader charged a great thick root with one blow like an axe -- 'twas enough to fell the tree to the ground, and the boars waiting below tore the hermit to pieces and gnawed the bones clean in a moment. Then they perched the Carpenter's Boar on the tree-trunk, filled the dead man's shell with water, and sprinkled him to consecrate him for their king, with a young sow for his Consort -- the origin, says the story, of the custom that a king at his crowning is set on a fine chair of fig-wood and sprinkled out of three shells.

title.en: Macch-uddana: The Fish Worth a Thousand

region.en: The bank of the Ganges (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 恆河岸畔（象徵標記）

texts.period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: A thieving younger brother swaps a parcel of gravel for the family money and drops the 'gravel' overboard; the Ganges spirit, fattened on the merit of a meal-gift, has a fish swallow the parcel, sells it to the wronged brother for seven annas -- and even the Bodhisatta still sends the cheat his half.
summary.zh: 兄弟收債千枚歸途，兄臨眠以餘食擲河飼魚，功德歸於河神，河神神力增長。弟欲獨吞，以碎石包調換錢包。船至中流，弟佯跌，將『碎石包』墮水，實為錢包。河神令大口魚吞之。弟歸家啟包，唯見碎石，心如枯木。漁人獲魚，索價千枚七分，人人笑之；至菩薩門前只索七分。妻剖魚得錢。河神現身說明原委，並勸勿分與弟；菩薩仍遣人送五百枚與弟。

passages.text: When Brahmadatta reigned in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into the family of a landed proprietor. At their father's death he and his young brother went to a village to arrange some business and were paid a thousand pieces of money. On the river-bank, waiting for the boat, they ate a meal out of a leaf-pottle, and the Bodhisatta threw what he left into the Ganges for the fishes, giving the merit to the river-spirit, who accepted it with gratification, and by the increase of her divine power became aware what had happened.

The young brother was of a thievish nature, and wanted the money for himself: he packed a parcel of gravel to look like the parcel of money and put them both away. At mid-river he stumbled against the side of the boat and dropped overboard the parcel of gravel -- as he thought, but really the money. 'Brother, the money's overboard! What's to be done?' 'What can we do? What's gone is gone; never mind about it,' replied the other. But the river-spirit resolved to take care of his property, and by her power made a big-mouthed fish swallow the parcel. At home the cheat chuckled over his trick -- and undid the remaining parcel to find nothing but gravel; his heart dried up and he fell on his bed clutching the bedstead.

Some fishermen casting their nets took the fish by the spirit's power and carried it to town to sell. 'A thousand pieces and seven annas,' they asked, and everybody laughed; brought to the Bodhisatta's door, they let him have it for seven annas. His wife cut it open, and there was the parcel of money; he knew his mark. 'Who could believe the story, were he told, that fishes for a thousand should be sold?' he marvelled -- and at the moment the river-spirit hovered invisibly in the air: 'I am the Spirit of the Ganges. You gave the remains of your meal to the fishes and let me have the merit; therefore I have taken care of your property. There lies your brother, his heart dried up. There is no prosperity for the cheat: do not give it to him.' 'That is impossible,' said the Bodhisatta, and all the same sent the brother five hundred.

title.en: Supatta: The Crow Who Gave His Life

summary.en: Queen Crow Softie craves a taste of the king's own cooking; Captain Prettybeak strikes the dinner-carrier's nose to make him drop the dishes, spends his life gladly for his king and queen -- and wins the white umbrella, the king's adhesion to the Crow-king's counsel, and daily food for eighty thousand crows.
summary.zh: 鴉王蘇波陀（美翅）統八萬烏鴉棲於波羅奈城郊。鴉后軟兒忽思王廚之食，思之欲死。隊長美喙自願捨身取食：令四鴉銜飯、四鴉銜魚侍奉王后，自撲膳夫，啄鼻塞口，飯盡落地。國王擒之，聞其捨身之由，嘆曰：『人尚不能為我捨生，烏鴉竟爾！』遂賜白傘。鴉以傘回敬，讚王后之美德。國王從其教，日煮大釜之飯以飼眾鴉，行善護生，其遺訓七百年猶存。

passages.text: When Brahmadatta was king in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born a crow, and became chief of eighty thousand crows, Crow king Supatta, Fairwing, with his mate Suphassa, Softie, and his captain Sumukho, Prettybeak. Passing over the king's kitchen, Softie smelt the odour of a host of dishes of fish, uncovered a moment to cool, and longed for a taste; the next day she told her lord she must have some of the king's food, or die.

King Crow sat down to think, and Prettybeak asked if aught displeased him. 'Oh, that will be all right,' said the captain: 'stay where you are today, and I will fetch the meat.' He gathered the crows, posted them in companies to watch near the kitchen, and with eight champions sat on the kitchen roof: 'When the food is taken up, I will make the man drop the dishes -- and that is an end of me. Four of you must fill your mouths with the rice and four with the fish, and feed our royal pair; if they ask where I am, say I am coming.' The cook hung his dishes on a balance-pole and went towards the king's rooms; in the court the captain flew and settled on the carrier's chest, struck him with extended claws, pecked the end of his nose with his spear-point beak, and stopped up his jaws with his two feet.

The king, walking on an upper floor, saw it all: 'Down with the dishes and catch the crow!' The man dropped the dishes and caught the crow tight; the crows ate all they wanted and carried off the rest as they had been told, till the craving of Softie was appeased. 'You have broken my servitor's nose and thrown away your life; what made you do such things?' asked the king. 'O great king, our king lives near Benares and I am captain of his forces. His wife conceived a great longing; at once I devoted my life; now I have sent her the food, and my desire is accomplished.' The king marvelled that a crow should sacrifice life for his king, gave him the white umbrella; and the crow saluted the king with the gift and praised the virtues of Fairwing. The king sent for him, heard his teaching, fed king and queen on the food he ate himself, and had a large measure of rice cooked daily for the crows; and the admonitions of Fairwing were remembered for seven hundred years.
